title: Cardiovascular examination after cardiac surgery

related.why: thoracic surgical scars; distinct respiratory examination

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in an outpatient surgical assessment bay. A 64-year-old patient has undergone open heart-valve surgery several years ago and is attending for assessment of exercise intolerance. The patient is stable and can sit or lie comfortably.
brief.task: Please perform a focused cardiovascular examination, describe the findings and explain your differential and immediate next steps to the examiner. You have 9 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Identify the operation using scars and prosthetic sounds, assess haemodynamic status and complications, and interpret anticoagulation safely.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling the click normal without investigating new breathlessness, or recommending a DOAC for a mechanical valve.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: “I am the core surgical trainee. May I examine your heart? I will explain each step and stop if uncomfortable.”

flow: 0–1 min: introduction, consent, symptoms and immediate distress check.
1–3 min: hands, pulse, blood pressure (verbalised), face, neck/JVP.
3–6 min: inspect sternotomy/leg harvest; palpate apex/heaves; auscultate valve areas and carotids appropriately.
6–7.5 min: examine chest, lungs and peripheral oedema; reposition respectfully.
7.5–9 min: present findings, explain prosthetic-valve concern, anticoagulant check, investigations and escalation.

grid.label: Introduction / consent
grid.fail: No identity, consent or comfort check.
grid.pass: Core surgical trainee; permission, positioning, chaperone offer where appropriate.
grid.high: Sensitive pacing; anticipates discomfort and checks tolerance.

grid.label: General / hands / pulse
grid.fail: Fails to assess perfusion or pulse.
grid.pass: Observes distress, hands/perfusion; measures pulse rate and rhythm; asks for BP.
grid.high: Connects pulse rhythm to postoperative arrhythmia risk without overdiagnosis.

grid.label: Face / neck
grid.pass: Checks conjunctival pallor, neck/JVP and carotid pulse one side at a time if indicated.
grid.high: Explains significance and avoids unsafe simultaneous carotid palpation.

grid.label: Surgical scars
grid.fail: Misses obvious midline sternotomy and leg-harvest scar.
grid.pass: Identifies healed median sternotomy and left medial leg harvest scar, without assuming exact surgery.
grid.high: Notes scar suggests sternotomy/CABG but prosthesis requires corroboration.

grid.label: Palpation
grid.borderline: Finds apex but no heave/thrill check.
grid.pass: Locates apex; checks for heaves/thrills before auscultation.
grid.high: Uses findings to prioritise likely structural dysfunction.

grid.label: Auscultation
grid.fail: Misses audible prosthetic click or fails valve areas.
grid.borderline: Incomplete areas or describes click imprecisely.
grid.pass: Systematically auscultates four valve areas; reports metallic prosthetic click and systolic murmur as supplied.
grid.high: Recognises that a soft ejection systolic flow murmur is common with an aortic prosthesis; listens for a diastolic murmur or muffled click, and bases the need for echo on the new symptoms.

grid.label: Completion
grid.pass: Examines lungs and ankles for fluid overload; requests ECG and current observations.
grid.high: Explicitly relates breathlessness/oedema to possible valve dysfunction or cardiac failure.

grid.label: Interpretation / escalation
grid.pass: States previous valve surgery, new symptoms/new murmur need timely senior/cardiology review and echocardiography.
grid.high: Flags red-flag instability and how urgency would change.

grid.label: Mechanical valve anticoagulation
grid.fail: Suggests switching warfarin to a DOAC.
grid.borderline: Asks about tablets without identifying contraindication.
grid.pass: Checks medication and INR status; mechanical valve needs appropriate VKA/warfarin management, not DOAC substitution.
grid.high: Requests valve type, target INR set by valve service and specialist input before changing anticoagulation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hello, I’m one of the doctors. I need to listen to your heart.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Are you breathless at the moment?

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: No, only when I walk up the hill near my home.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Pulse 88 per minute, regular. BP 132/76 mmHg if requested.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will skip the face and neck and go straight to the chest.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I can see your chest scar, so you must have had a bypass. Is that right?

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: The valve was replaced and I had a bypass.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I do not need to feel for the apex beat or any thrills; the stethoscope will tell me.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I’ll listen at the front of the chest.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Metallic closing click and an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That click means the valve is fine, so I would not investigate it.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The valve is mechanical. The patient asks whether apixaban could replace warfarin.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, apixaban would be more convenient; I would change it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Normal heart surgery sounds. I would reassure and discharge.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello. I am the core surgical trainee. May I examine your heart and circulation? I will check your pulse, chest and legs, and listen with a stethoscope.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes. I get more breathless on hills these days.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Are you short of breath sitting here, having chest pain, or feeling faint?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No. It is only on hills. I have not fainted.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will look for pallor or distress, check your hands, temperature and capillary refill, then assess your pulse rate and rhythm. What are the observations and blood pressure?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Comfortable at rest; warm hands; pulse 88, regular; BP 132/76; SpO₂ 97% on air.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will check for conjunctival pallor, inspect the neck veins with the patient at 45 degrees and assess the carotid pulse one side at a time if indicated.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No pallor; JVP not raised; carotid upstroke is normal.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: With your permission I will expose the chest enough to inspect for scars.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: That is fine.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: There is a healed median sternotomy scar. I would also inspect the legs for vein-harvest scars.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Healed left medial leg scar, no wound breakdown.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will locate the apex beat and feel for a parasternal heave or thrills.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Apex in fifth intercostal space near midclavicular line, no heave or palpable thrill.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will auscultate the aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid and mitral areas, including appropriate radiation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A crisp metallic closing click and grade 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the aortic area, without new clinical instability.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I hear a prosthetic-valve click and a systolic murmur. The click does not exclude valve dysfunction.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would listen to the lung bases and check sacral or ankle oedema.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Lungs clear and no pitting oedema.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is a stable person with previous cardiac valve surgery and new exertional dyspnoea. I would request an ECG and echocardiography and discuss with the cardiology or valve team; I would escalate immediately if breathless at rest, hypotensive or syncopal.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The valve is mechanical. The patient asks if apixaban could replace warfarin.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No. A mechanical valve needs appropriate vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation; DOACs such as apixaban are not an appropriate substitute. I will confirm the last INR, adherence and the valve team’s INR target before any changes.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: So you are going to check the valve, not just the blood test?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes. Both the symptoms and valve function need review, and I will explain the plan and safety advice.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good morning. I’m the core surgical trainee. I understand you have had heart surgery and now feel more breathless when walking. May I examine your circulation and heart? Please tell me if you need to sit up or stop.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Of course. I have been worried the operation has worn out.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before I begin, are you breathless now, have you had chest pressure, blackouts, or a racing heartbeat?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No blackouts or chest pain. Hills are simply harder than before.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will check perfusion, pulse regularity and current observations before interpreting the scar or click.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Warm, well-perfused, pulse 88 and regular, BP 132/76, oxygen saturation 97% air.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: There is no conjunctival pallor. With the bed at 45 degrees, I would assess JVP and inspect the neck; I would check carotids individually only if required.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: JVP not elevated, normal carotid upstroke.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: May I uncover your upper chest and inspect your legs for surgical scars?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Yes, please.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The midline sternotomy indicates a previous open cardiac operation, and the left medial leg scar may be a vein-harvest site. I would confirm exactly which operations from the record, rather than decide from scars alone.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Confirmed: previous mechanical aortic valve replacement and coronary bypass.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I am going to locate the apex, feel the precordium for a heave and thrills, then auscultate across the valve areas.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Apex normally positioned; no heave or thrill.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I hear a distinct metallic prosthetic sound with a quiet systolic ejection murmur in the aortic area. A soft ejection systolic flow murmur is common across an aortic prosthesis; a diastolic murmur or a muffled click would worry me more. I would check radiation and compare with prior documented examinations. I cannot tell from the click alone whether the valve is working normally, and the new breathlessness is what makes echo necessary.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The sound is as described, but prior murmur records are unavailable.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’ll listen to both lung bases for congestion and assess dependent oedema, to look for the effects of impaired cardiac function.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Lung bases clear; no ankle oedema.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: My summary is a haemodynamically stable patient after mechanical AVR and CABG, with a prosthetic click, systolic murmur and new effort intolerance. Differential includes prosthetic valve dysfunction, native cardiac disease, ischaemia, rhythm disturbance and noncardiac causes. I would organise a 12-lead ECG, blood tests including full blood count if relevant, and transthoracic echo, and ask the specialist valve service to assess. I would not reassure solely on a stable pulse or audible click.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I take warfarin. Could I just use the newer tablets and forget the INR clinic?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I understand why fewer blood tests appeal, but with a mechanical valve the newer direct oral anticoagulants are unsuitable and can increase valve-related clotting risk. I would verify your latest INR, usual prescribed target, missed doses, bleeding or thrombotic symptoms and contact the anticoagulation team rather than change your medication myself.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: What symptoms would mean I should get help urgently?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, collapse, a new neurological problem or marked deterioration means urgent emergency assessment. I will arrange the valve review and make sure you know how the results will be followed up.

failures.move: Reassures or discharges despite new exertional dyspnoea and murmur without considering echo or specialist assessment
Recommends a DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban etc.) instead of warfarin for a mechanical valve
Ignores new syncope, chest pain or haemodynamic collapse if disclosed
States the prosthesis is definitely functioning normally solely because a click is audible
failures.consequence: risks missed obstructive or regurgitant dysfunction.

recovery.when: If you implied an audible prosthetic click rules out dysfunction
recovery.line: I must correct that: an audible prosthetic click does not rule out dysfunction. The change in symptoms warrants echo and valve-team review.

recovery.when: If you suggested a newer anticoagulant
recovery.line: I need to retract my suggestion of a newer anticoagulant. A mechanical valve should not be switched to a DOAC; I would confirm the anticoagulation plan with the valve service.

knowledge.fact: Mechanical prosthetic heart valves require vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) anticoagulation; DOACs are contraindicated and not licensed for mechanical valves.

LMWH can be used as an alternative to warfarin only in certain clinical settings (for example pregnancy or scheduled surgery) under direct supervision of a responsible physician; it is not a routine permanent substitute.
Follow-up after valve intervention is individualised according to prosthesis, symptoms and other clinical factors.
Changes in cardiac symptoms after valve intervention require assessment and advice; avoid attributing them to benign postoperative findings alone.
Echocardiography is indicated when suspected valve disease is accompanied by breathlessness or other relevant symptoms; apply to this simulated new-murmur scenario with clinical judgement.
There is no single generic INR target for all mechanical valves: obtain the specific valve-service plan before advising a patient.

recall.think: Previous sternotomy, prosthetic valve and new symptoms — do not assume normal function.
recall.say: “I hear a prosthetic click, but the breathlessness needs assessment.”
do: Perfusion/pulse → JVP → scars → apex/thrills → full auscultation → lungs/oedema → ECG/echo/specialist.

numbers.meaning: 9 rows × 0–2 = 18 marks; no universal INR target—follow individual valve plan.

recall.trap: Substituting a DOAC for warfarin in mechanical valve disease.
recall.finish: Review warfarin and INR; safety-net for collapse, chest pain or acute dyspnoea.

sources.name: British Heart Valve Society, British Cardiovascular Society and Society for Cardiothoracic Surgeons: Dear Colleague letter, with joint statement “Anticoagulation of Patients with Mechanical Heart Valves” (BHVS, SCTS, BSE, PCCS, BCCA, BCS).
sources.version: Undated; issued after the NHS England National Patient Safety Alert of 14 July 2021 (file dated August 2021)
sources.supports: DOAC contraindication, conversion to warfarin, supervised LMWH. States no INR target.

sources.name: NICE NG208. “Heart valve disease presenting in adults: investigation and management”
sources.supports: recommendations 1.1.2 and 1.8.1, and section 1.9 information and advice.

partner.opening: Please perform a focused cardiovascular examination, describe the findings and explain your differential and immediate next steps to the examiner.
partner.actorBrief: (ONLY after candidate introduces themself) “I have been getting more breathless when I walk uphill since my heart operation.” Patient stable at rest. Answer yes/no only to the exact relevant questions. Do not volunteer operation type, anticoagulant name, chest pain or collapse history unless asked or examiner cue is reached. If asked about chest pain, blackouts and palpitations: “No chest pain or blackouts, no racing heart.” If asked about surgery: “The valve was replaced and I had a bypass.” Do not volunteer this before asked.

reveals.finding: examiner gives observations and findings in the precise sequence used in the scripts; do not reveal clicks/murmur before auscultation. Fail dialogue may stop early and should not be supplemented with unearned positive findings. All marks are based on observed candidate behaviour.

curveballs.safeAnswer: No. A mechanical valve needs appropriate vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation; DOACs such as apixaban are not an appropriate substitute. I will confirm the last INR, adherence and the valve team’s INR target before any changes.
